desc: This station involves the immediate management of an abnormal CTG during an oxytocin induction that is complicated by umbilical cord prolapse, followed by examiner questions on fetal position, the cardinal movements of labour and how to talk to a woman during shoulder dystocia.
explain:
Abnormal CTG: the first steps

An abnormal CTG in labour is a trigger for early help, together with a short set of simple measures: change the woman's position, check and correct maternal hypotension, stop oxytocin or other uterotonics if hyperstimulation is suspected (and consider tocolysis), check temperature (sepsis screen if above 38 °C), check the signal (reposition the transducer or apply a fetal scalp electrode), and perform a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse. If the trace remains abnormal, fetal scalp stimulation or fetal blood sampling can be considered, or birth expedited. Here the trace showed a prolonged deceleration in the setting of oxytocin, tachysystole and recent amniotomy with a high presenting part, so stopping oxytocin and repositioning are first, and a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse is mandatory.

Umbilical cord prolapse

Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency, with risk factors including a high or unengaged presenting part, malpresentation, polyhydramnios, prematurity and recent artificial rupture of membranes. The cord is compressed between the presenting part and the pelvis, and may also go into vasospasm if handled. Management is:

  • Call for help immediately and assess the fetal heart rate.

  • Relieve cord compression by elevating the presenting part with gloved fingers. If birth will be delayed (e.g. during transfer), fill the bladder.

  • Position the woman knee-chest or left lateral head-down.

  • Handle the cord as little as possible.

  • Consider acute tocolysis only as an adjunct, e.g. while contracting or if birth will be delayed.

  • Prepare for birth. None of these steps may delay it, which is usually by category 1 caesarean.

Fetal position and the cardinal movements

Position is the relationship of the denominator (the occiput in a vertex presentation) to the maternal pelvis. LOA means the occiput lies towards the left and front of the maternal pelvis, the most common and favourable position for birth. The cardinal movements are: engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution and external rotation, and expulsion (delivery of the anterior shoulder, then the body, with lateral flexion).

Shoulder dystocia: communication

When the head is born but retracts against the perineum and the body does not follow, shoulder dystocia is suspected. The woman should be told clearly that her baby's head is born but a shoulder is stuck behind her pubic bone, asked to stop pushing (because pushing may worsen impaction and the manoeuvres, not pushing, release the shoulder), and told that more help is being called and her position will be changed. Staff should explain each manoeuvre as it happens.
focus: Intrapartum obstetric emergency: shoulder dystocia, cord prolapse and abnormal CTG in labour
guide:
A high-performing candidate will call for senior help straight away, run through the first steps for an abnormal CTG without delay (stop oxytocin, reposition, correct hypotension, vaginal examination), and recognise a cord prolapse when they feel it. They will elevate the presenting part, keep it elevated, position the woman head-down, avoid handling the cord, and call a category 1 caesarean with no delay. They will talk to the woman throughout. In the examiner questions they will define LOA accurately, list the cardinal movements in the right order, and give a clear shoulder dystocia script that includes stopping pushing.

A borderline candidate may find the abnormal CTG but miss one of the first measures (usually stopping oxytocin, or the vaginal examination), or may not call for help early. They may identify the cord prolapse but not keep the presenting part elevated, or may forget the head-down position. They may hold off on calling the caesarean until after other steps, or fail to explain what is happening to the woman. In the questions they may swap the order of the cardinal movements or tell the woman to keep pushing.
patient:
Profile:

  • Name: Maria Costa.

  • Age: 29-years-old.

  • Gender: Female (she/her).

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: No.

  • Location: Birth suite.

Background (role-player):

  • First baby was a normal vaginal birth at term, 3.4 kg, no complications.

  • This pregnancy: uncomplicated, induced for post-dates. No known allergies. No medications other than the oxytocin infusion and epidural.

  • You are anxious and ask, "Why has everyone rushed in? Is the baby okay?"

  • If you are told clearly and kindly, you agree to any examination or position change. If the student does not explain, you ask "What are you doing?" and become more distressed.

  • If you are asked to go on all fours or knee-chest, you can do so with help, despite the epidural.

  • If the student explains that you need an urgent caesarean, you say "Okay, just please get my baby out safely. Can my husband come with me?"

Examiner findings (provide only when asked):

  • Fetal heart rate: baseline 140 bpm earlier; now 70 bpm for 3 minutes, then slowly recovering to 100 bpm if oxytocin is stopped and the woman is repositioned, but not to baseline.

  • Contractions: 6 in 10 minutes, each lasting about 90 seconds on palpation (tachysystole) on the oxytocin infusion.

  • Observations: pulse 105/min, BP 84/50 mmHg (after epidural top-up), temperature 37.1 °C, SpO2 98% on room air. Improves to 102/62 mmHg after left lateral position and IV fluid bolus.

  • Transducer signal: adequate, no loss of contact.

  • Vaginal examination (when performed): a loop of pulsating umbilical cord is felt below the presenting part. Cervix 5 cm. Vertex at station -2, LOA. Membranes ruptured, clear liquor. The cord pulsates at about 70 bpm.

  • If the presenting part is elevated: the fetal heart rate improves to around 110 bpm.

  • Theatre: the obstetric registrar and anaesthetist are en route. Category 1 caesarean is called when requested.

Examiner questions for Task 3 (ask verbatim):

  1. "The midwife wrote 'LOA' in the notes. What does each letter stand for, and what does fetal position describe?"

  2. "Name the cardinal movements of labour in order."

  3. "With a different woman, the baby's head is born but retracts against the perineum and the body does not follow. What do you say to her?"
points: For an abnormal CTG, call for help early, alongside the first measures: reposition, correct hypotension, stop oxytocin for hyperstimulation, check temperature, check signal and perform a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse.
In cord prolapse, elevate the presenting part, position head-down, handle the cord minimally and proceed to category 1 caesarean without delay.
LOA describes position: the occiput (denominator) lies left and anterior in the maternal pelvis.
The cardinal movements are engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution/external rotation and expulsion.
In shoulder dystocia, tell the woman to stop pushing and explain what is happening while the manoeuvres are performed.

stem:
You are a final-year medical student on placement on the birth suite of a metropolitan hospital. You are in the room with the midwife, Sam, who is looking after Mrs Maria Costa, a 29-year-old G2P1 at 39+4 weeks. She is having an induction of labour for post-dates concerns and is on an oxytocin infusion. Her membranes were ruptured artificially 20 minutes ago, and her last vaginal examination, done at that time, found 5 cm dilatation with the vertex at station -2, LOA. She has a working epidural. Her last blood pressure 15 minutes ago was 110/65 mmHg.

Over the last 10 minutes the CTG has changed. The baseline was 140 bpm with normal variability. There is now a prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm that has lasted 3 minutes, and the midwife counts 6 contractions in 10 minutes. The midwife asks you to help while the registrar is paged. The registrar is 10 minutes away.
tasks: Describe your immediate steps for this abnormal CTG, and what you would do and say to the woman, as the examiner provides findings (3 minutes).
Manage the problem you identify on examination, including explaining to Mrs Costa what is happening and what will happen next (3 minutes).
Answer the examiner's questions about fetal position, the cardinal movements of labour and communication during shoulder dystocia (2 minutes).
title: Abnormal CTG on the birth suite
